summary: Proposes a coordination mechanism for MPLS-TP pseudowire dual-homing local protection. The two dual-homing provider edge nodes use it to exchange state and coordinate switchover. It builds on the framework in RFC 8184.

plainLanguage.summary: Two guards watching two doors need to tell each other what is going on, so they agree on which door to use.

questions: what is a dhc message in mpls-tp
how does pseudowire dual-homing protection work
subtitle: How two provider edge routers sharing one customer link tell each other about failures so they switch together.

tldr.problem: When a customer site is dual-homed to two provider edge nodes, an access link failure should be handled locally at those nodes, without moving the working pseudowire or triggering massive switchover in the network.
tldr.mechanism: The two dual-homing PEs send Dual-Homing Coordination (DHC) messages to each other over a Dual-Node Interconnection pseudowire, carrying either the service PW status or a switching request, and follow a shared forwarding state table.
tldr.outcome: Both PEs agree on which service PW is active, so traffic keeps flowing despite a failure in the attachment circuit, a PE or the packet switched network. It defines a new G-ACh channel type and a TLV registry.

today: RFC 8185 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the coordination companion to the framework in RFC 8184.

sections.title: Why Dual-Homing Needs Coordination
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection (RFC 6372, RFC 6378, RFC 7771) protects an LSP or pseudowire between edge nodes, but not against failure of the attachment circuit (AC) or of the edge nodes themselves. Pseudowire redundancy (RFC 6718, RFC 6870) covers those by adding edge nodes, but needs a PW switchover on an AC failure and relies on PSN protection for PW failure.

In scenarios such as mobile backhauling, the customer edge (CE) on one side is dual-homed to two provider edge (PE) nodes. Operators prefer to switch locally at the dual-homing PEs and keep the working PW unchanged when they can. That avoids massive PW switchover in the backhaul network, which could cause congestion by moving traffic off planned paths. Likewise, when one working PW fails, keeping the working AC avoids needless switchover for other PWs that share it.

RFC 8184 gives the framework and scenarios; this RFC adds the coordination mechanism for static MPLS-TP PWs. The text states the mechanism has been implemented and deployed in several mobile backhaul networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If one door is blocked, it is better for the two guards to just switch doors themselves than to reroute everyone in the whole city.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
On the single-homing side the usual linear protection is unchanged. On the dual-homing side, the working PW ends on one PE and the protection PW on the other. As RFC 8184 describes, a dedicated Dual-Node Interconnection PW (DNI-PW) joins the two dual-homing PEs and forwards traffic between them.

Each dual-homing PE has a forwarder that connects the AC, the service PW and the DNI-PW. For linear protection to work across two nodes, the PEs must coordinate how the forwarder is set. The working and protection roles come from the management system or local configuration.

On the single-homing PE, the working and protection PWs are treated as if they end on the same remote node, so normal MPLS-TP protection coordination still applies. The state of the service PW comes from OAM between the PEs and the remote PE, and the DNI-PW state comes from OAM between the dual-homing PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each guard has a hallway linking their door to the other guard's door, and a switch that decides where visitors go.

sections.title: The Forwarding State Table
sections.content:
Each dual-homing PE decides what to forward from three inputs: the service PW is Active or Standby, the AC is Active or Standby, and the DNI-PW is Up or Down. The RFC's Table 1 gives the result.

  • With the DNI-PW up: service PW and AC both active means Service PW <-> AC; service PW active with AC standby means Service PW <-> DNI-PW; service PW standby with AC active means DNI-PW <-> AC; both standby means drop all packets.
  • With the DNI-PW down: only service PW and AC both active still forwards (Service PW <-> AC); every other combination drops all packets.

The AC status comes from existing AC redundancy mechanisms, and the DNI-PW status from PW OAM as defined in RFC 5085. Both are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A little rule chart tells each guard where to send visitors depending on which doors work. If the hallway between them is broken, they only let people through if their own door and route are both fine.

sections.title: The DHC Message and Its TLVs
sections.content:
Coordination messages travel on the DNI-PW over the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh, RFC 5586), using a new channel type, 0x0009, assigned by IANA. The Dual-Homing Coordination (DHC) message starts with the 4-octet common G-ACh header, then a 4-octet Dual-Homing PEs Group ID that MUST be the same on both PEs in a group, then a TLV length (the total length of the TLVs that follow) and the TLVs.

Two TLVs are defined:

  • PW Status (type 1, 20 bytes): reports the sender's service PW status. It holds the destination and source PE Node_IDs (32 bits, usually the LSR ID, per RFC 6370), the 32-bit DNI-PW ID, flags, and a Service PW Status field. The P flag bit says whether the sender is the working PE (0) or protection PE (1). In the status field the F bit signals Signal Fail and the D bit Signal Degrade, either local or received from the remote PE.
  • Dual-Node Switching (type 2, 16 bytes): sends protection state coordination. It has the same Node_ID and DNI-PW ID fields and flags with P and S bits. The S bit says which service PW carries traffic: 0 for the working PW, 1 for the protection PW.

Other flag bits are reserved: they MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The guards send each other short notes. One kind says "my road is broken" and the other says "let's switch to the other road."

sections.title: Sending Rules and Failure Scenarios
sections.content:
When a PE sees a change in service PW status, it MUST put it in a PW Status TLV and send it to the other PE as quickly as possible using three consecutive DHC messages, so that fast switching still works if one or two are lost or corrupted. Afterwards it MUST keep sending its latest status periodically. When a PE decides the active service PW must move from working to protection, it MUST do the same with the Dual-Node Switching TLV, setting the S bit. The RECOMMENDED default interval for the three rapid messages is 3.3 ms, similar to RFC 6378, and the default for later messages is 1 second; both SHALL be operator-configurable.

The RFC walks through PE1 (working) and PE2 (protection) with a remote PE3:

  • Normal state: PW1 and AC1 active, PW2 and AC2 standby, so traffic uses PW1 and AC1 only.
  • AC1 fails: AC2 becomes active, the PWs are unchanged. PE1 forwards between the working PW and the DNI-PW, and PE2 between AC2 and the DNI-PW. Only the AC switches.
  • PW1 fails in the PSN: if PE1 sees it, PE1 MUST send the PW Status TLV to PE2 and make PW1 standby. PE2 SHOULD make PW2 active and tell PE3 via a protection coordination message. If PE3 sees the failure, it tells PE2 over PW2, and PE2 SHOULD send a DHC message with the S bit set, which also covers a unidirectional failure PE1 cannot detect.
  • PE1 fails: PE2 and PE3 both detect it and SHOULD make PW2 active, AC2 becomes active and PE2 forwards between PW2 and AC2.

Because the DNI-PW carries both DHC messages and service traffic during switching, multiple diverse links between the PEs are RECOMMENDED, and underlying LSP protection SHOULD be enabled. PSN tunnel protection is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: When something breaks, a guard shouts the news three times fast so it is not missed, then keeps repeating it calmly. The other guard then picks up the visitors.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned G-ACh channel type 0x0009 for the MPLS-TP Dual-Homing Coordination message and created an "MPLS-TP DHC TLVs" subregistry with 0x0001 PW Status (20 bytes) and 0x0002 Dual-Node Switching (16 bytes). The allocation policy is IETF Review (RFC 8126).

DHC messages carry control information. If an attacker injects or modifies one, the PEs might disagree on which should deliver CE traffic, which could be used for denial of service against the CE. The RFC says to use DHC messages within a trusted MPLS-TP domain (RFC 6941), and notes the message inherits the security of the G-ACh. Injecting messages requires subverting a transit node, which it calls generally hard and impossible to protect against at the protocol level, so management-level techniques are more appropriate. Identifiers must be unique, which is the assigner's job.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster slips fake notes between the guards, they might disagree about which door to use. So the hallway has to be in a place only trusted people can reach.

fields.desc: G-ACh channel type assigned by IANA.

fields.name: Dual-Homing PEs Group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the dual-homing group; the same at both PEs.

fields.desc: Total length in octets of the TLVs that follow.

items.desc: 20 bytes. Reports service PW status, with P, F and D bits.

items.desc: 16 bytes. Coordinates switchover, with P and S bits.
